items.stem: What is inflation?
options: A sustained increase in the general price level
A fall in the price level
A rise in the price of one good
items.answer: A sustained increase in the general price level
items.markingKey: Ongoing rise in average prices.

items.stem: Explain how a consumer price index is constructed.
items.answer: A base year is chosen (index = 100); a household expenditure survey selects a representative basket and weights; prices are collected regularly; price changes are weighted and averaged to give the index.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basket/survey; 1 mark: weights; 1 mark: base year/index calculation [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between deflation and disinflation.
items.answer: Deflation is a fall in the general price level (negative inflation); disinflation is a fall in the rate of inflation while prices are still rising.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: The table shows a simplified consumer price index for Umbria Nova. Category: Transport, Food, Energy; Weight: 30, 50, 20; Price change (%): 8, 10, 10. Calculate the rate of inflation.

The table shows a simplified consumer price index for Quentara. Category: Transport, Entertainment, Clothing; Weight: 40, 35, 25; Price change (%): 3, 3, 4. Last year the CPI was 120. (a) Calculate the weighted inflation rate and the new value of the CPI. (b) Explain why the weighted rate differs from a simple average of the price changes. (c) Explain why this inflation rate may not reflect the experience of every household.
items.answer: (a) +3.25%; CPI = 123.9. (b) Categories with larger weights (bigger share of spending) influence the index more; the simple average is 3.33%. (c) Households’ spending patterns differ from the average basket (e.g. low-income households spend more on food).
items.markingKey: (a) weighted average [2]; new CPI [1] (b) weights [1] (c) different baskets [1] [5]

items.stem: The table shows a simplified consumer price index for Istrana. Category: Energy, Clothing, Food; Weight: 50, 30, 20; Price change (%): −2, 5, 4. Last year the CPI was 100. (a) Calculate the weighted inflation rate and the new value of the CPI. (b) Explain why the weighted rate differs from a simple average of the price changes. (c) Explain why this inflation rate may not reflect the experience of every household.
items.answer: (a) +1.3%; CPI = 101.3. (b) Categories with larger weights (bigger share of spending) influence the index more; the simple average is 2.33%. (c) Households’ spending patterns differ from the average basket (e.g. low-income households spend more on food).
items.markingKey: (a) weighted average [2]; new CPI [1] (b) weights [1] (c) different baskets [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: The CPI in Zentara was 120 two years ago, 123 last year and 130 this year. Energy prices rose sharply after a global supply shock, and the central bank warns of a wage–price spiral. Average wages rose by 4% this year. Pensioners and savers complain that their living standards are falling. (a) Calculate the approximate change in real wages this year. (b) Explain why pensioners and savers lose from inflation.
items.answer: (a) −1.7% (b) Fixed nominal incomes and low interest rates mean falling real incomes and real value of savings.
items.markingKey: (a) 4 − 5.7 [1] (b) Credit: Fixed nominal incomes and low interest rates mean falling real incomes and real value of savings. [3]

items.stem: Extract: The CPI in Jovania was 120 two years ago, 123 last year and 130 this year. Energy prices rose sharply after a global supply shock, and the central bank warns of a wage–price spiral. Average wages rose by 4% this year. Pensioners and savers complain that their living standards are falling. (a) Calculate the inflation rate in each of the two years. (b) Calculate the approximate change in real wages this year. (c) Explain whether the inflation is more likely to be demand-pull or cost-push.
items.answer: (a) +2.5%, +5.7% (b) −1.7% (c) Cost-push: energy supply shock raised costs (SRAS left).
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: +2.5%, +5.7% [2] (b) 4 − 5.7 [1] (c) Credit: Cost-push: energy supply shock raised costs (SRAS left). [2]

items.stem: Explain two limitations of a CPI as a measure of inflation.
items.answer: Basket and weights may not match all households; quality changes and new products; substitution when prices change; excludes some items (e.g. housing costs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each limitation explained [4]

items.stem: What causes demand-pull inflation?
options: Aggregate demand rising faster than aggregate supply
items.answer: Aggregate demand rising faster than aggregate supply
items.markingKey: Too much spending chasing too few goods.

items.stem: Explain the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation, using AD/AS analysis.
items.answer: Demand-pull: AD shifts right near full capacity, raising the price level (and output). Cost-push: higher costs shift SRAS left, raising the price level and reducing output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each; 1 mark diagram reference [3]

items.stem: Explain how inflationary expectations can cause inflation to persist.
items.answer: If people expect prices to rise, workers demand higher wages and firms raise prices in advance, so costs and prices continue rising.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: wage demands; 1 mark: firms’ pricing [2]

items.stem: World oil prices double, raising firms’ costs in Halvoria. Which type of inflation is most likely?
items.answer: Cost-push inflation
items.markingKey: Cost-push inflation: higher costs shift SRAS left.

items.stem: Trade unions in Valdoria win wage increases well above productivity growth. Which type of inflation is most likely? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Cost-push inflation: higher unit labour costs raise prices.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Cost-push inflation; 1 mark: explanation – higher unit labour costs raise prices. [2]

items.stem: Identify the type of inflation in each case and explain. (i) World oil prices double, raising firms’ costs in Pelora. (ii) An export boom and rapid credit growth push spending in Pelora above capacity.
items.answer: (i) Cost-push inflation (ii) Demand-pull inflation
items.markingKey: (i) Cost-push inflation – higher costs shift SRAS left. [2] (ii) Demand-pull inflation – excess AD. [2] Total [4]

items.answer: Cost-push: an SRAS shift left raises prices and reduces output; demand-pull would normally raise output too.

items.stem: Who is most likely to lose from unanticipated inflation?
options: Savers whose interest rate is below the inflation rate
items.answer: Savers whose interest rate is below the inflation rate
items.markingKey: Real value of savings falls.

items.stem: Explain two costs of inflation.
items.answer: Redistribution from savers and those on fixed incomes; menu and shoe-leather costs; uncertainty reduces investment; loss of international competitiveness; fiscal drag.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cost, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why a period of deflation can increase the burden of debt.
items.answer: Debts are fixed in money terms; as prices and incomes fall, the real value of the debt rises, making repayment harder.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed nominal debt; 1 mark: real burden rises [2]

items.stem: Amara saves $5,000 for a year at a nominal interest rate of 5%. Inflation over the year is 6%. What is the approximate real interest rate?

Arjun saves $5,000 for a year at a nominal interest rate of 3%. Inflation over the year is 8%. (a) Calculate the nominal value of the savings after one year and their real value in today’s prices. (b) Explain who gains and who loses from this situation.
items.answer: (a) $5,150; real value $4,768.52 (less than $5,000). (b) Savers lose purchasing power; borrowers gain because the real value of what they repay falls.
items.markingKey: (a) nominal [1]; real ÷ (1 + inflation) [1] (b) savers vs borrowers [2] [4]

How is a nominal value converted into a real value?
items.answer: Nominal value ÷ price index × 100
items.markingKey: Deflating by the index (base = 100).

items.stem: A worker’s wage rises from $500 to $550 while prices rise by 10%. What has happened to the real wage?
items.answer: It is unchanged
items.markingKey: 10% rise in wage = 10% inflation.

items.stem: Explain why it is important to use real values when comparing incomes over time.
items.answer: Nominal incomes may rise just because of inflation; real values show changes in purchasing power, i.e. what the income can actually buy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflation distorts; 1 mark: real = purchasing power [2]

items.stem: What is disinflation?

A fall in the general price level
A rise in the inflation rate

items.answer: (a) ≈ +2.9% (b) Higher unit labour costs reduce profit margins; firms raise prices and SRAS shifts left, raising the price level. (c) If output per worker rises as fast as wages, unit labour costs are unchanged, so there is no cost pressure on prices.

items.stem: Newspapers in Calvania have recently reported a lively debate among economists on this issue. Assess whether cost-push inflation is harder for a government to control than demand-pull inflation.
items.answer: For: Reducing AD to fight cost-push worsens unemployment/output (stagflation); causes often external (oil prices). Against: Demand-pull can be persistent with credit booms; supply-side policies help cost-push; credible central bank anchors expectations; depends on cause. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Reducing AD to fight cost-push worsens unemployment/output (stagflation); causes often external (oil prices). Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Demand-pull can be persistent with credit booms; supply-side policies help cost-push; credible central bank anchors expectations; depends on cause. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.answer: (a) +2.5%, +5.7% (b) −1.7% (c) Fixed nominal incomes and low interest rates mean falling real incomes and real value of savings.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: +2.5%, +5.7% [2] (b) 4 − 5.7 [1] (c) Credit: Fixed nominal incomes and low interest rates mean falling real incomes and real value of savings. [3]

items.stem: In a revision note Nadia wrote: ‘If my wage rises by 5%, I am 5% better off.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: Only if prices are unchanged; the real change is roughly the wage rise minus the inflation rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Only if prices are unchanged; the real change is roughly the wage rise minus the inflation rate. [2]

items.stem: In Lunaria, the average weekly wage rose from $500 to $540 while the CPI rose from 120 to 132 (base year = 100). Calculate the real wage in the second year at base-year prices.

In Selmaria, the average weekly wage rose from $500 to $540 while the CPI rose from 100 to 112 (base year = 100). (a) Calculate the real wage in each year at base-year prices. (b) Calculate the percentage change in the real wage. (c) Explain what this shows about workers’ living standards.
items.answer: (a) $500 → $482.14 (b) −3.6% (c) Real wages fell: wages did not keep up with prices, so purchasing power fell.
items.markingKey: (a) both real wages [2] (b) [1] (c) interpretation [1] [4]
